🍽️ Zomato Bangalore — Restaurant & Rating Insights

Data cleaning, exploratory analysis, and platform recommendations from 56,000+ restaurant listings

12,248Unique Restaurants
93Localities
2,541Cuisine Combinations
3.62Avg. Rating (of rated)

1. Data Cleaning Summary

What the raw export looked like, and how it was fixed before analysis

  • Corrupted rows removed: ~4,472 of 56,252 rows (≈8%) were unrecoverable — leaked fragments of review text (e.g. ('Rated 4.0', 'RATED... )) had spilled across every column due to unescaped quotes in the source export. These were detected because their rate field didn't match a valid pattern and were dropped entirely.
  • Rating field: stored as text like 4.1/5, 3.9 /5 (inconsistent spacing), NEW, or -. Extracted the numeric score to a clean rating float; NEW/- (no reviews yet) mapped to missing rather than zero.
  • Cost field: approx_cost(for two people) had comma-formatted numbers (e.g. "1,200") stored as text — converted to numeric ₹.
  • Categorical noise: a handful of rows had garbage values leaked into listed_in(type); restricted to the 7 valid categories (Delivery, Dine-out, Desserts, Cafes, Drinks & Nightlife, Buffet, Pubs and Bars).
  • Deduplication: the same restaurant appears multiple times in the raw file — once per listing type it's tagged under (Delivery, Dine-out, etc). For restaurant-level questions (location, cuisine, price), deduplicated on name + address → 12,248 unique restaurants, of which 9,064 have at least one rating.
  • Booleans: online_order and book_table Yes/No mapped to 1/0 for correlation analysis.
  • Text fields (cuisines, dish_liked, rest_type) are comma-separated multi-value strings — exploded into one row per value where needed (e.g. a "North Indian, Chinese" restaurant counts toward both cuisines).

2. Rating Landscape

How ratings are distributed once "NEW"/unrated listings are excluded

Ratings cluster tightly between 3.4 and 4.0 — very few restaurants score below 2.5 or above 4.5, suggesting either genuine consistency in Bangalore's dining scene or (more likely, per industry norms) rating inflation/selection bias, since restaurants that survive long enough to accumulate reviews tend to be decent.

3. Cuisine vs. Rating

Asian, American, BBQ and Salad-focused cuisines rate highest on average (3.9–4.06), while high-volume staples like Desserts, North Indian, and Fast Food rate lower — likely because they compete in a much larger, more price-sensitive, more saturated segment. Niche/premium cuisines have fewer but more satisfied customers.
North Indian (4,908 restaurants) and Chinese (3,504) dominate by sheer volume — together appearing in roughly half of all listings — followed by South Indian, Fast Food, and Biryani.

4. Location Hotspots

Whitefield, BTM, HSR and Marathahalli have the highest restaurant density (tech-corridor / residential hubs), but density doesn't equal quality — high-volume areas like Whitefield and Marathahalli sit mid-pack on average rating (~3.5), while quieter but more affluent/curated areas rate higher on average once you filter to areas with 50+ restaurants.

5. Price vs. Rating

Cost for two correlates positively with rating (r ≈ 0.31). Restaurants above ₹1,000/head for two average 4.05–4.12 vs. 3.54–3.57 for budget places under ₹600. This likely reflects better service, ambience, and consistency at higher price points — not that expensive food simply "tastes better."

6. Online Order, Table Booking & Restaurant Type

Table-booking-enabled restaurants rate notably higher (avg. 4.09 vs 3.57) — table booking is a strong proxy for full-service, sit-down establishments (vs. QSR/cloud kitchens), which correlates with better experiences. Online-order availability shows a much weaker relationship with rating (3.64 vs 3.58) — it's now table stakes rather than a differentiator.
Fine Dining, Microbreweries and Lounges rate highest among common formats, while Quick Bites and Delivery-only kitchens — the largest segment by count — rate lowest, reinforcing the price/format/rating link above.

7. Correlation Heatmap — What Drives Rating

Votes (r=0.38), table booking (r=0.36) and cost (r=0.31) are the strongest positive correlates of rating. Table booking and cost are themselves highly correlated (r=0.59) — both are markers of the same "full-service, higher-price" restaurant profile. Online order has almost no correlation with rating (r=0.08).

8. Location × Cuisine Heatmap

Cross-referencing the top 10 localities against the top 10 cuisines surfaces pockets of excellence — e.g. Continental and Cafe cuisine tend to outperform their citywide average in Indiranagar and Koramangala, upscale/nightlife-oriented neighborhoods, versus more modest ratings for the same cuisines in outer, high-density areas like Electronic City.
The count view shows where supply is concentrated: North Indian and Chinese saturate almost every neighborhood, while cuisine diversity (Continental, Cafe, Desserts) is more unevenly distributed — a signal for where a platform could nudge under-served demand.

9. Popular Dishes

Pasta, Burgers, Biryani, Pizza and Coffee are the most frequently name-checked "liked dishes" across restaurants — a mix of comfort-food staples (Biryani, Paratha) and café/casual-dining items (Pasta, Coffee, Sandwiches), reflecting Bangalore's blend of traditional and cosmopolitan dining habits.

10. Recommendations for an Alfido Tech–Style Platform

Actionable ideas based on the patterns above — partnerships, content, and product angles

Partnerships

1. Court niche, high-rating cuisines rather than chasing volume categories

Asian, BBQ, American and Continental restaurants rate 0.2–0.3 points higher than the North Indian/Fast Food segments that dominate by count. A platform can differentiate by building preferred-partner programs (better placement, lower commission tiers) with these smaller-but-stronger cuisine categories, rather than competing purely on North Indian/Chinese volume where Zomato/Swiggy already have deep supply.

Content

2. "Hidden Gems by Neighborhood" content series

The location × cuisine heatmap shows specific cuisine-neighborhood combinations that outperform the citywide average. A recurring content/social series ("Best Continental in Koramangala," "Top-rated Cafes in Indiranagar") built directly from this data gives users discovery value competitors' generic "top rated near you" lists don't, and doubles as SEO content.

Product

3. Promote table-booking as a trust signal, not just a convenience feature

Table-booking-enabled restaurants rate half a point higher on average and are the single strongest behavioral correlate of quality in this dataset. Surfacing "Table Booking Available" as a filter/badge (rather than burying it as a feature toggle) helps users self-select into higher-satisfaction experiences, and gives the platform a lever to push more restaurants toward adopting booking.

Partnerships

4. Target under-served but high-density areas for expansion incentives

Whitefield, Marathahalli, Electronic City and Bellandur have huge restaurant counts (tech-corridor demand) but below-average ratings and are dominated by budget/delivery formats. This is a case for partnering with a handful of well-rated fine-dining/microbrewery operators to open outposts there — filling a "no good place to eat after work" gap that the data suggests exists.

Content / Monetization

5. Price-tier-based curated lists, marketed honestly

Since cost for two correlates with rating (r≈0.31) largely because pricier restaurants are fuller-service, a "best of ₹300 budget eats" list needs different quality expectations than a "best of ₹1,500+ experiences" list. Segmenting recommendation content and restaurant scorecards by price tier — rather than one universal rating — sets more accurate user expectations and creates natural ad/sponsorship tiers for restaurant partners at each price point.

Analysis based on the Zomato Bangalore restaurants dataset (56,252 raw rows → 47,356 valid listings → 12,248 unique restaurants, 9,064 rated). Built with pandas, matplotlib & seaborn.
